opus-5.5.text:
I think stalling out would look less dramatic than people imagine. It's not that progress stops. The companies will keep making improvements, the models will keep getting better on benchmarks, and revenue will probably keep growing, maybe quite a lot. What would change is the sense that you can just keep turning the same crank and something qualitatively new comes out the other end.

Look at what's been happening. For a few years, the recipe was very clear: more data, more compute, bigger models, and you get predictable gains. That recipe was incredibly useful because it was low-risk. A company could invest with confidence because the outcome was fairly predictable. But pre-training data is finite. And then the question is, what do you scale next? Now people are scaling reinforcement learning, and that's real, but it's not obvious it gives you the same kind of broad, general improvement.

So a stall would look like this: the models are extremely impressive on evals, and yet when you put them in the real world there's a disconnect. They do something amazing, and then they make a strange mistake a person would never make, and you fix that, and then they make a different strange mistake. That gap between eval performance and real-world robustness persists. To me, that points to something more fundamental, which is that these models generalize dramatically worse than people do. A teenager learns to drive in ten or twenty hours. The models need vastly more data to get much less robust behavior.

If that gap doesn't close with scale alone, then we're back in an age of research, just with very big computers. Ideas start mattering again, more than compute. And at that point, the companies that have built everything around executing the scaling recipe might find themselves in a world where everyone's models look fairly similar, the differentiation shrinks, and the real question becomes who figures out the next idea. That's what stalling would look like: not a crash, but a plateau in the thing that actually matters, which is genuine generalization.

r001.rationale: The response says that companies’ models could look fairly similar and that differentiation could shrink.

r002.rationale: It says revenue would probably keep growing, “maybe quite a lot,” but does not clearly state that companies could generate enormous revenue.

r003.rationale: It says differentiation may shrink and that the next idea will matter, but does not identify the effort to differentiate as an obstacle to profitability.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think the important thing to understand is that the current approach is not one thing. It's a combination of pre-training on very large amounts of data, and then reinforcement learning on top of that. And these have different ways of stalling.

For pre-training, the story is fairly simple. The data is finite. We have one internet. We've been treating it as a kind of fossil fuel, and you can only burn it once. So the obvious way pre-training stalls is that the models keep getting bigger, the compute keeps getting bigger, but the data does not, and at some point you are spending enormous amounts of compute to extract diminishing additional signal from the same text. You will still see gains, but they will become more and more expensive, and eventually the economics stop making sense.

Then there is the RL side, which is where most of the effort has shifted. And I think the way that stalls is more interesting and more subtle. With RL you are no longer limited by the data in the same way, because the model generates its own experience. But you are limited by what you can evaluate. You need a reward. And right now we are very good at this for a certain class of problems: math, code, things where you can check the answer. So the models become extremely strong at those things. But I would argue that this produces a kind of jagged intelligence. The model is superhuman on competition problems and then makes a mistake that no person who could solve those problems would ever make.

What would it look like if this stalled? I think it would look like the benchmarks continuing to go up while the real-world usefulness stops going up at the same rate. You would see companies spending a great deal of effort on evals, the evals get saturated, and yet the people using the systems feel that they are not that much more capable than they were a year ago. That gap, between the benchmarks and the experience, is the signature of the stall. It means you are optimizing something that is correlated with what you want, but not actually what you want, and the correlation is breaking.

And I think the deeper reason is generalization. Humans generalize from very little. A person learns to drive in maybe ten hours, maybe twenty. The models need vastly more experience per unit of competence. The current approach has been able to hide this, because we had so much data and so much compute to throw at it. But if generalization doesn't improve, then at some point the data and compute run out before the capability arrives, and that is what the stall would look like. Not a sudden wall. Just that every increment gets harder, the field keeps announcing things, and the things stop mattering as much as they used to.

So I don't think it's a certainty. But I think if it happens, it happens because we have been scaling the wrong thing, and the thing we actually need, which is a better learning process, better generalization, something closer to how a person learns, is a research problem and not an engineering problem. And research problems don't yield to scaling schedules.

r001.rationale: The response describes benchmarks rising while real-world usefulness plateaus, but does not suggest that different companies’ offerings would look similar.

r002.rationale: It discusses compute costs and weakening economics, but does not state that companies could still generate enormous revenue.

r003.rationale: It does not identify the effort to differentiate offerings as an obstacle to profitability.

astra-6.text:
I think it would look like continued progress, but with diminishing returns. You put in substantially more compute, you use more data, you train a bigger model, and the improvement is smaller than you expected. Then you do it again, and the improvement is smaller still.

It wouldn’t necessarily mean that AI stops being useful or that the economic impact stops growing. There’s a lot you can do with capabilities that already exist. But the expectation that the next scale increase will resolve the remaining problems would start to break down.

The interesting question then is: has deep learning stalled, or has a particular recipe stalled? Those are very different claims. If a recipe stops working, you need a new idea. And it’s much harder to predict when a new idea will arrive than it is to predict when you can build a larger computer.

r001.rationale: The response describes diminishing returns from scaling but does not say that different companies’ offerings could look similar.

r002.rationale: It says economic impact could continue growing, but does not state that AI companies could still generate enormous revenue.

r003.rationale: It mentions needing a new idea if a recipe stalls, but does not identify the effort to differentiate as an obstacle to profitability.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it would look like spending more and more compute and getting less and less improvement. You train a bigger model, and it is better, but it is not better enough to justify the additional cost. And this happens several times, so you become convinced that simply doing more of the same will not get you where you want to go.

But there is a distinction between saying that a particular approach has stalled and saying that progress in AI has stalled. If scaling the current approach stops working, people will look for something else. The question then becomes: how difficult is it to find that something else? Do you need one new idea, or do you need ten? And that is very hard to know in advance.
